children: Karnataka High Court says ED had sufficient grounds to seize Genpact’s Gurgaon property under FEMA, while leaving the question of an actual violation to the competent authority.

The Karnataka High Court has upheld the Enforcement Directorate's action to seize a Genpact property in Gurgaon under India's foreign exchange law, finding that the agency had sufficient material to form a "reason to believe" that warranted action under the Foreign Exchange Management Act.

The ruling, delivered on September 16 by Justice Suraj Govindaraj, relates to a series of transactions involving Genpact India and its overseas group companies in 2015, followed by payments running into thousands of crores from India to overseas entities.
The court, however, made clear that it was not deciding whether Genpact had ultimately violated FEMA. That determination will have to be made by the competent authority under Section 37A of the law.
At the centre of the Enforcement Directorate's investigation are transactions involving Empower India, Genpact India and overseas Genpact entities.

According to the judgment, Genpact Bermuda borrowed USD 737.5 million from Morgan Stanley in March 2015. The funds were routed through Genpact Luxembourg, which subscribed to 4,600 non-convertible debentures issued by Empower India for about Rs 4,600 crore.

Empower India transferred the entire amount on the same day to acquire the remaining 51 per cent stake in Genpact India. The funds were subsequently transferred to Genpact Singapore and then Genpact Bermuda, which used the money to repay the Morgan Stanley borrowing.
The ED argued that the transactions formed part of a connected arrangement and amounted to a circular movement of funds.
The court held that the agency was entitled to examine the transactions as a connected arrangement rather than considering each transaction separately.

The judgment also records that Genpact India made payments of around Rs 7,800 crore to Genpact Luxembourg between 2018 and 2023 towards repayment of the principal and interest on the non-convertible debentures.

The court said these subsequent transactions could be examined as part of the arrangement under investigation, even though Section 37A could not be applied retrospectively to transactions that took place before the provision came into force.
On the seizure of Genpact's Gurgaon property, the court found that the ED's order contained sufficient material for the authorised officer to form the requisite "reason to believe" under Section 37A.
"At this stage, the court is not called upon to determine whether there is a contravention of FEMA," the judgment said, adding that the issue would have to be decided by the competent authority.
Genpact had also pointed to proceedings involving the Reserve Bank of India, the Securities and Exchange Board of India and income-tax authorities.

The High Court said those proceedings did not prevent the ED from independently examining the transactions under FEMA, noting that they had not determined whether the entire arrangement, viewed as a whole, constituted a violation of Section 4 of FEMA.
The court therefore dismissed Genpact's challenge to the seizure.
It did, however, set aside the ED's rejection of Genpact's application for a no-objection certificate for a proposed USD 100 million investment in its GIFT City entity.
The court directed the competent authority to reconsider the application and issue a reasoned order.
The ED was represented by Additional Solicitor General N. Venkataraman and other counsel, including Senior Advocate Madhu N. Rao.
